A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same audio-visual camera-pose estimation work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and supplementary sections are readable and can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v3 reports original experiments on Ego-Exo4D and HM3D-SS, including benchmark comparisons, component ablations, corruption tests and supplementary IMU and temporal analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds audio-corruption and alignment controls, further performance analyses, and manually annotated acoustic distributions.

M1.justification: The MUSIC++ DOA representation, learned binaural features, late fusion with Reloc3r, training losses and implementation architecture remain unchanged. Clarifying the HM3D-SS microphone count and the monaural ablation's retained DOA input does not establish a procedural change.

E1.justification: Ego-Exo4D, HM3D-SS and their visually corrupted variants remain the underlying coverage. v4 extends evaluation to noisy and geometrically mismatched audio, omnidirectional sound, and explicitly selected reliable-vision cases; it adds no underlying dataset.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the corresponding experiments, including Reloc3r, its AV variants, Chance, NA-CP, DOA-CP, SLfM on HM3D-SS, and the existing ablation and IMU variants. Newly cited vision methods are not evaluated as baselines.

E3.justification: Retained benchmark splits, metrics and training settings are unchanged. Added protocols introduce Gaussian audio noise at inference, 1–5-second audio offsets, within-scene shuffling, cross-scene replacement, and reliable-vision selection using structural similarity and ground-truth motion. Noise strength and several selection thresholds are not specified.

E4.justification: Sections 5.2 and 7.1 substantially expand analysis through controls testing geometric correspondence versus scene correlations, audio-noise and omnidirectional-sound robustness, and failures under reliable vision. Section 7.2 and new Table 9 also extend qualitative acoustic tags into quantitative distributions. The earlier ablations and robustness analyses remain.

E5.justification: v4 newly documents sample-based estimation of acoustic prevalence: Table 9 percentages come from 500 randomly sampled, manually annotated clip pairs per category and are extrapolated across the dataset. Existing significance assertions remain unchanged; no repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or additional significance-test specifications are introduced.

E6.justification: Existing numerical values in Tables 1–8 remain unchanged, but substantial new findings are reported: noisy-audio AUC@5/10/20 of 0.78/2.88/8.62; alignment-control AUC@5 of 0.68, 0.66 and 0.50 versus 0.81 synchronized; omnidirectional-sound gains of 8%/6%/3%; and wins in 95% of reliable-vision cases. Table 9 adds acoustic frequencies and setting counts, while Table 4b adds near-field tags for Music and Rock Climbing.

T1.justification: The mathematical task definition, feature-fusion formulations and losses in Equations 1–2 retain their substance. New geometric explanations and applicability arguments are qualitative, with no added formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and central conclusion retain the same claims: passive spatial audio complements vision, the combined DOA and binaural representation improves pose estimation, and the method establishes real-world audio-visual results. Additional evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations linking success to geometric audio alignment and late fusion, plus limitations involving silence, diffuse sources, unrelated soundtracks and untested cross-device generalization. It also newly suggests single-microphone applicability, although its clarified monaural ablation still uses DOA spectra, leaving that interpretation unsupported by the reported comparison.

D1.justification: v4 newly discloses eight NVIDIA A40 GPUs with 48 GB each, two microphones for HM3D-SS, retained DOA inputs in the monaural ablation, and annotation sampling and the greater-than-50% tagging threshold. These improve documentation without establishing changes to the retained implementations or training settings.

R1.justification: v4 adds references to MUSt3R, MASt3R, MegaSaM and Project Aria, and explains pairwise pose estimation's relationship to multiview systems and online operation. The central positioning around passive audio versus active echolocation remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Localized edits define in-the-wild footage, clarify terminology and task motivation, expand results and annotation explanations, and correct wording. Acknowledgements and a hardware section are added, while the overall narrative and section organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v4 adds the color-coded distribution Table 9, separates corrupted vision from audio-plus-corrupted-vision rows in Table 1, expands Table 4b's caption, and resizes or relocates existing displays. The underlying images in Figures 1–4 and the corruption examples are retained.

improvement.justification: Compared with v3, the alignment controls, additional robustness analyses and quantified acoustic annotations provide useful evidence about when audio helps or harms, while hardware disclosure improves transparency. The gain is limited by incompletely specified new test settings and the unsupported single-microphone interpretation despite retained DOA inputs. These additions improve the unchanged core study without establishing a substantial overall quality advance.
